1.0.0.en: “The proverbs of Solomon the son of David, king of Israel” [1].

1.0.1.en: The name of Solomon appears in three parts of this book (Prov 1:1; 10:1; 25:1). The ancient commentators regarded the whole book as the work of Solomon the Wise. It is said in (1 Kgs 4:32): “He spake three thousand proverbs: and his songs were a thousand and five,” and some scholars still take this view.

1.0.2.en: The word “proverb,” as we saw before, means in Hebrew “to rule” or “to govern” a matter, and some see that it means “to present a thing or a person by what resembles it.” It is as though this is the book in which Solomon the Wise presents the life of faith as God governs it in us and through us in practical reality.

1.0.3.en: Solomon mentions his name, his descent from his father David and his office as king of Israel, in order to declare his longing that we imitate him and become sons of peace, belonging to the Son of David, the true King, and become through Him kings and priests to God His Father (Rev 1:8).

1.0.4.en: Solomon points to himself in verse 1 as the king, the son of David. And we look to Wisdom Himself, the Son of David, the King of kings, and by acquiring Him we carry wisdom within us.

1.0.5.en: * He is a wise son of a wise father; therefore he added the name “David,” who begot Solomon. From childhood he learned the Holy Scriptures, and he received his authority neither by lot nor by violence, but by the judgment of the Spirit and by a divine decree.

1.1.0.en: 2 To know wisdom and instruction; to perceive the words of understanding; 3 To receive the instruction of wisdom, justice, and judgment, and equity; 4 To give subtilty to the simple, to the young man knowledge and discretion. 5 A wise man will hear, and will increase learning; and a man of understanding shall attain unto wise counsels: 6 To understand a proverb, and the interpretation; the words of the wise, and their dark sayings. 7 The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction.

1.1.1.en: Verses 2-6 tell us why Solomon wrote these proverbs. In brief, these proverbs support us in practicing wisdom in a practical way, so that we enjoy true success and lasting happiness. When a young man is concerned about his life, wants to walk as is fitting, recognizes his own ignorance, and longs to learn and to enjoy knowledge, then he receives knowledge, understanding and discernment.

1.1.2.en: Ten words are used in verses 2-4 which seem to be synonyms. Certainly there is a relationship among them, but these synonyms differ from one another. Among these words are:

1.1.3.en: A. Wisdom, chochmah: in the Bible it means “the ability to use knowledge rightly.” It is used 37 times in this book alone, and it is a word of importance in the Bible. Perhaps wisdom means not only the divine knowledge by which we can discover the best end of man’s life and how we can reach it by fitting ways, but it also means the heavenly teaching by which we discover ourselves as we come to know God, so that wisdom guides us into all truth and forms true religion in its entirety. Wisdom brings us into true and practical knowledge, for there are many people gifted with extraordinary intelligence and having knowledge, but they lack wisdom, and so they misuse knowledge.

1.1.4.en: Wisdom is the subject and the aim of God’s school. And wisdom in the Old Testament means Jesus Christ for the contemporary believer. “But of him are ye in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption” (1 Cor 1:30).

1.1.5.en: When you come to know the Lord Christ, you reject playing with folly and corruption, and you become wise. And when you receive the Lord Christ into your life, you enter into new experiences of knowledge and are truly reckoned wise.

1.1.6.en: B. Instruction, musar: it appears 26 times in the Book of Proverbs. The literal meaning is teaching or correction by discipline, as in (Prov 13:24): “He that spareth his rod hateth his son: but he that loveth him chasteneth him betimes” (cf. Prov 3:11; 22:15).

1.1.7.en: Discipline here is for teaching and not for punishment and vengeance (Eph 4:14; 2 Pet 1:6). For God, in His love for the sinful man, hands him over for a time to the fruit of his works, not to take vengeance on him, but that he may taste the bitterness and death that sin brings, and so come to himself and return to God his Savior, who lifts him out of sin; thus the soul is reformed. This is what we also should do, as fathers or leaders: to carry a spirit of love and self-giving even toward the one we discipline. For sadly, criminals are sometimes thrown into prison to be reformed, while we punish our children with anger and violence. We discipline criminals to reform them, while we punish our children as though we were taking vengeance on them. This is a kind of confusion, and a failure of our hearts to open wide to the new generations.

1.1.8.en: C. Knowledge: it is true and useful information. The verb “to know” is used about a thousand times in the Old Testament.

1.1.9.en: The Bible affirms that faith is not opposed to knowledge, for faith is offered to man as a rational being who is eager to enjoy true knowledge. St. Clement of Alexandria says: “Here are the observations that form our gnosis (knowledge): first contemplation, then the fulfillment of the commandments, and finally the instruction given by the righteous. When these things are realized in a person, he becomes a gnostic (one who has knowledge).”

1.1.10.en: D. Understanding: the believer who receives the Lord Christ, “Wisdom,” into his life and responds to discipline receives an understanding of God’s plan for his life.

1.1.11.en: * Understanding is the eye of the soul; therefore the word “Israel” means: “the one who sees God, that is, the one who understands God.

1.1.12.en: St. Clement of Alexandria E. Justice: it is righteousness, and means walking uprightly.

1.1.13.en: F. Judgment (truth): it means to pass judgments or take wise decisions, as children of God fulfilling His will. Every day the believer stands at a crossroads to decide where to go in his life. This needs divine help and heavenly wisdom.

1.1.14.en: G. Equity: it means spiritual integrity. Here it points to a principle rather than a way of behavior.

1.1.15.en: The children of God are not subject to rulings, but are given principles to guide them on the way. As it is said in Rom 14:22: “Happy is he that condemneth not himself in that thing which he alloweth.” The believer carries strong inner feelings that lead him toward the truth, though he realizes that many times he is walking on eggshells, and he needs inner help to lead him so that he does not fall.

1.1.16.en: H. Discretion (discernment): it means discerning between the good and the evil, the precious and the worthless, the beneficial and the harmful. Believers enter God’s school so that they may become God’s children: wise, righteous and honored.

1.1.17.en: “To know wisdom and instruction; to perceive the words of understanding” [2].

1.1.18.en: He begins with knowledge to affirm the link of faith with knowledge; then he links wisdom with instruction. If wisdom is God’s school, which translates true knowledge into upright behavior (practical wisdom), the believer will not attain this without bowing to God’s disciplines, which straighten the soul and develop understanding. The believer needs teaching, training and refinement, and by this he receives a true understanding of God’s plan for him.

1.1.19.en: * As for wisdom and instruction [2], it is said that wisdom is the knowledge of all human and divine things and of their causes; therefore whoever is a practicing theologian knows wisdom. “Howbeit we speak wisdom among them that are perfect: yet not the wisdom of this world, nor of the princes of this world, that come to nought: But we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, even the hidden wisdom, which God ordained before the world unto our glory” (1 Cor 2:6, 7).

1.2.0.en: St. Basil the Great “To receive the instruction of wisdom, justice, and judgment, and equity” [3].

1.2.1.en: Here he clarifies the preceding statement, affirming that the purpose of wisdom is to receive discipline with joy, to obtain knowledge that satisfies the heart and mind, and righteousness, which is walking in a spirit of uprightness, and to acquire truth and equity.

1.2.2.en: Thus the wise man reveals the living relationship between the divine Teacher and the believing disciple. For the Teacher’s aim is not merely the acquiring of noble behavior, but the enjoyment of divine knowledge, righteousness and heavenly truth in an integrated, upright life that touches the whole being of the believer: his heart, mind, will, feelings and all his behavior, hidden and visible. It is the disciple’s enjoyment of the icon of his divine Teacher, Wisdom Himself!

1.2.3.en: St. Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, sees that these divine gifts of knowledge, justice, judgment and equity transform the soul into a garden full of spiritual fruit, or into a bride who bears the beauty of her bridegroom.

1.2.4.en: * How delightful is this garden whose fruits represent the beauty of the Bridegroom!

1.2.5.en: He is the true light, the true life, the true righteousness, and so on, as Wisdom says.

1.2.6.en: When a person comes to possess these qualities through good works, he looks upon the cluster (of virtues which) belongs to his conscience, and sees the Bridegroom there, reflecting the light of truth by his pure life.

1.3.0.en: St. Gregory, bishop of Nyssa “To give subtilty to the simple, to the young man knowledge and discretion” [4].

1.3.1.en: The word “discretion” in Hebrew appears in the plural, “counsels,” and it is used of the pilot of a ship who holds the rudder in his hand, moving and steering it as he wishes. So by wisdom the believer becomes the leader of his thoughts and the steersman of his inner life, guiding the ship of his life by the Holy Spirit of God in the royal way.

1.3.2.en: The word is also used of the tending of sheep, where a man tends all his energies and abilities like a flock that listens to him.

1.3.3.en: Adam Clarke sees that the word “simple” is used in more than one sense. It means the plain-hearted, those who walk with clarity and openness, who show outwardly what they are inwardly. Here simplicity carries the meaning of innocence, absence of guile, and not harming others. But since very few people came to carry this trait, the word was misused and turned into the idea of foolishness, lack of wisdom and inexperience. Here the word is used in the latter sense.

1.4.0.en: “A wise man will hear, and will increase learning; and a man of understanding shall attain unto wise counsels” [5].

1.4.1.en: These proverbs were written not only for the young but also for the wise, for it is fitting that they grow in wisdom by being ready to be taught. It is fitting that they be willing to listen and not content with themselves. For even in guiding others they need to hear and learn. As St. Ambrose says, all humanity needs to learn; God alone teaches and does not need to learn.

1.4.2.en: A person in humility bows to listen to the voice of wisdom, feeling the need for constant growth in knowledge. Thus he says with St. Paul the Apostle: “He speaks wisdom among them that are perfect” (1 Cor 2:6). And as the Lord Christ says, that to him who has, it is given and he has more; so the wise man, by his longing to learn, increases in wisdom, and the fool, by his refusal to learn, increases in ignorance and folly.

1.5.0.en: “To understand a proverb, and the interpretation; the words of the wise, and their dark sayings” [6].

1.5.1.en: If wisdom cries out on the high places and goes down into the markets to offer the free invitation of salvation in simplicity to every person, she nevertheless keeps some hidden mysteries, which she presents as a gift to those who are earnest in seeking them and asking for them from God.

1.5.2.en: God does not scatter pearls on the ground, and the precious jewels He hides from human eyes so that they may seek them and find them. Gold and pearls and everything precious are sought in mines and in the depths of the earth, and petroleum is extracted from the depths. So God hides His mysteries so that we may realize that they are worth seeking by study with prayer. As the Lord Christ says: “Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have life.”

1.5.3.en: The call of the Book of Proverbs to us today: Dig! Study deeply, so that you may declare to God your earnest longing to enjoy the gift of wisdom and understanding, and He will reveal to you the mysteries of His word.”

1.5.4.en: What does he mean by dark sayings (chidoth)? Some believe that he means by this the parables that our Lord Jesus Christ presented.

1.5.5.en: After reviewing the purpose of wisdom, he presented to us the motto of the whole book, which is:

1.6.0.en: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction” [7].

1.6.1.en: This verse is the key to the book. I have already pointed to the meaning of “the fear of the LORD.”

1.6.2.en: Here there is a contrast between the fear of the Lord, which urges the believer to learn, and folly, which does not want to learn from wisdom but rejects it as it rejects instruction.

1.6.3.en: The first foundation that must be laid for erecting the spiritual building is the fear of the Lord. What destroys it is the madness of relying on one’s own will, with unwillingness to learn, along with disobedience and the rejection of all counsel and all discipline. Besides knowing what is good and what is evil, which the fear of the Lord achieves, one must submit to the order God has set, by governing the will and sanctifying it through submission to parents, true leaders and counselors.

1.6.4.en: What is the relationship between the fear of the Lord and true wisdom?

1.6.5.en: Are there not among the atheists, or at least among those who deny the faith, some who have attained high degrees of knowledge? We do not deny that some of those who ignore the existence of God, and even blaspheme His name and despise His word, have high knowledge of many languages, or are well versed in scientific knowledge, or have obtained academic degrees in philosophy, politics, history and so on. This knowledge may be useful, and sometimes it harms if it drives a person to pride and arrogance even against the Creator Himself. But true fear supports a person in his relationship with God and with his brothers, and even with his body and soul, and opens before him the doors of hope in heavenly things, so that he lives in a spirit of joy and exultation; by this a person is reckoned truly wise.

1.6.6.en: * If the law brings fear, then the knowledge of the law is the beginning of wisdom, for a person cannot be wise without the law. Whoever despises the law is not wise, and is therefore reckoned wicked.

1.6.7.en: St. Clement of Alexandria * The arrogant and wrathful person becomes the prey of his successive passions through the loss of wisdom; therefore the prophet says: “There is no soundness in my flesh; my wounds stink and are corrupt because of my foolishness” (Ps 38:3, 4), showing that all sins begin with folly. So the virtuous man who has the fear of the Lord understands more than others, and as the wise man says: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” [7]. If the one who fears the Lord receives wisdom, and the wicked man does not have this fear, then he is deprived of true wisdom. And when he loses what is called true wisdom he becomes more foolish than others. Yet many admire the wicked, thinking that they are able to wrong and harm others, and they do not know that we must truly reckon these to be more wretched than all men, these who, while they think they are harming others, strike themselves with the sword. It is a work of extreme folly for a man to strike himself without knowing it, thinking that he hurts others while he is killing himself.

1.6.8.en: St. John Chrysostom * “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom”; the awareness of sin leads to repentance, and God grants His compassion to those who repent.

1.6.9.en: St. Irenaeus * (The philosophers) say that God must not be feared, for in their view all things are free and without any rule governing them.

1.6.10.en: Why is God not to be feared, unless because He does not exist?

1.6.11.en: If God does not exist, then truth does not exist either..

1.6.12.en: But where God exists, there is the fear of God, which is the beginning of wisdom.

1.6.13.en: And where the fear of God exists there is earnestness, honorable and balanced diligence, with careful watchfulness, a respected attachment (to holy service), a fellowship together full of trustworthiness, offering good service, submission (to authority), devout listening, humble running, a united Church, and God is in all things.

1.6.14.en: Tertullian Many of the Fathers see the believer’s need of the fear of the Lord, especially at the beginning of the way, for it is the guide of the body and the soul, with the mind and all the faculties, to walk in the royal way, to carry the person across into the divine presence, and to enjoy living fellowship with God. Therefore St. Gregory of Nazianzus warns us against beginning our spiritual life with contemplation of divine things without being bound by the fear.

1.6.15.en: * It is fitting for us not to begin with contemplation and leave the fear (for contemplation without restraint may perhaps drive us toward recklessness), but we must be established and purified, and become light through fear, and so be lifted up to the heights. For where there is fear the commandments are kept, and where the commandments are kept there is purity of the body, which is the cloud that covers the soul and hides from it the sight of the divine ray. And where there is purity there is illumination, and where there is illumination the desires of those who long for great things are satisfied, and for the greatest of things, that is, God, who surpasses all greatness.

1.6.16.en: St. Gregory of Nazianzus If the Book of Psalms was called in Hebrew “Tehillim,” that is, “the exultations,” because it is the book of the soul that exults in the Lord even in the midst of its sufferings and sorrows, then the expression “the fear of the LORD” is often repeated in it. For the fear of the Lord is linked with joyful shouting, and so the psalmist says: “Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling” (Ps 2:11). And in Psalm 115:11 true believers are called those who fear the Lord: “Ye that fear the LORD, trust in the LORD”; and it is said of the Lord Christ Himself, the incarnate Word of God: “And the spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the LORD, and his delight shall be in the fear of the LORD” (Isa 11:2, 3). It is as though the prophet invites us to share in this feature by our union with the Word, so that we carry the spirit of the fear of the Lord with delight and joy.

1.6.18.en: The word “fools” means the wicked, that is, the wicked in their hearts, in their thoughts and in their ways, those who rely on their own will and are hardened, unwilling to listen to any advice. And just as the wise man wants to learn eagerly, so the fool is the one who cannot bear to hear guidance that leads him toward true success and happiness.

1.7.s.en: 3. A warning against association with destructive groups (gangs)

1.7.0.en: 8 My son, hear the instruction of thy father, and forsake not the law of thy mother: 9 For they shall be a crown of grace unto thy head, and chains about thy neck. 10 My son, if sinners entice thee, consent thou not. 11 If they say, Come with us, let us lay wait for blood, let us lurk privily for the innocent without cause: 12 Let us swallow them up alive as the grave; and whole, as those that go down into the pit: 13 We shall find all precious substance, we shall fill our houses with spoil: 14 Cast in thy lot among us; let us all have one purse: 15 My son, walk not thou in the way with them; refrain thy foot from their path: 16 For their feet run to evil, and make haste to shed blood. 17 Surely in vain the net is spread in the sight of any bird. 18 And they lay wait for their own blood; they lurk privily for their own lives. 19 So are the ways of every one that is greedy of gain; which taketh away the life of the owners thereof.

1.7.1.en: “My son, hear the instruction of thy father, and forsake not the law of thy mother” [8].

1.7.2.en: The seven chapters are addressed to “my son.” This expression is used about 15 times. In these chapters we hear the heartbeats of a father who wants the best life for his son. It is the voice of the spiritual father, as it is the voice of the parents, that is, the voice of the Church and the voice of the family church.

1.7.3.en: It is fitting for us to realize that the relationship between the true teacher and his disciple is the relationship of a father to his son. Teaching in the early Church was an episcopal work, or a fatherly work. Teaching is not merely the presentation of doctrines and teachings, but the presentation of a living experience of the new life in Christ Jesus, which the disciples experience with their fathers.

1.7.4.en: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob were called “fathers” (patriarchs), or the fathers of Israel [(Gen 1:24) LXX, (Ex 3:13; Deut 1:8; Acts 3:13; 7:2, 12; Rom 4:12, 16; 2 Pet 3:4)]. According to Jewish tradition the official title of the scribes was “father.” And in the Church of the New Testament, at the martyrdom of St. Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, the Jews and the pagans cried out: “This is the father of the Christians.” And when Pope Athanasius the Apostolic referred to St. Dionysius of Alexandria, St. Dionysius of Rome and others, he used the word “the Fathers.”

1.7.5.en: Teaching and discipleship were inseparable from one another. Through true fatherhood the bishops and priests looked on teaching not as the fruit of theoretical doctrines, but as the fruit of their fatherly love, repeating the words of St. Paul: “For in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel” (1 Cor 4:15).

1.7.6.en: * When a person learns from the mouth of another, he is called the son of the one who teaches him, and the other is called his father.

1.7.7.en: St. Irenaeus * Speech is the son of the soul; therefore we call those who teach us our fathers.

1.7.8.en: St. Clement of Alexandria He refers here to the parents, and not to the father alone. Mothers and grandmothers have played a principal role in every age, down to our present age. Many great men enjoyed the wealth of blessings they learned at their mothers’ knees. Among these great mothers and grandmothers are Hannah, the wife of Manoah, the mother of Lemuel, Lois and Eunice, Mother Dolaji, St. Rebecca and St. Monica.

1.7.9.en: Not only is it fitting for children to honor their parents, but it is fitting for fathers also to realize their responsibility for teaching and training their children. The parents are supposed to have the fear of the Lord, able to offer the best counsel to their children, and to present to them an exact example of the godly life. For the counsel of the parents is in vain if their own conduct is not upright.

1.7.10.en: Usually the father gives instructions and imposes discipline, but he is not always present in the midst of the family because of work, while the mother is often within the doors; therefore the order of the family is bound up with her, and it is she who presents the law to her children.

1.8.0.en: “For they shall be a crown of grace unto thy head, and chains about thy neck” [9].

1.8.1.en: This phrase appeared in the Septuagint: “So thou shalt receive a crown of grace for thy head, and chains for thy neck” (LXX)

1.8.2.en: Respect and filial obedience create honor, glory and spiritual beauty in the life of the wise son. Obedience grants the adornment of grace to his head as a crown and a diadem, and golden chains and pearls.

1.8.3.en: The children of the nobles and aristocrats used to put a chain around their necks to distinguish them from the rest of the people. And here the Book of Proverbs directs our eyes to the fact that whoever listens to his father and accepts his disciplines becomes a nobleman among the noblemen.

1.8.4.en: * The crown is also made of a marvelous material.. of the tender mercies of God, for the psalmist says: “Bless the LORD, O my soul, who crowneth thee with mercy and compassion” (Ps 103:2, 4).

1.8.5.en: And it is made also of glory: “Thou hast crowned him with glory and honour” (Ps 8:6); “With blessing Thou hast crowned us as with a shield” (Ps 5:12) LXX.

1.8.6.en: And also of grace: “Thou shalt receive a crown of grace upon thy head” (Prov 1:9) LXX.

1.8.7.en: See this crown, which among many crowns surpasses the others in grace.

1.8.8.en: St. John Chrysostom In the Song of Songs we see the bride having adorned her neck with chains of obedience and of service to others, and it is said of her: “Thy cheeks are comely with rows of jewels (like a dove), thy neck with chains” (Song 1:9). A man’s neck without adornment often points to the coarseness of human nature, but if it is adorned with the gifts of the Holy Spirit it becomes a symbol of spiritual beauty and gentleness in bearing with others... These are the ecclesiastical chains (the collar or necklace). Our neck once bore shame and disgrace because of our disobedience and pride, but now it bears the yoke of Christ and accepts His obedience, and so it has come to bear surpassing spiritual beauty.

1.8.9.en: * “How beautiful are thy cheeks, as the cheeks of a dove, thy neck with chains” (Song 1:9)...

1.8.10.en: Let us interpret the neck of the bride... as pointing to the souls that have received the yoke of Christ, who says: “Take my yoke upon you... for my yoke is easy” (cf. Mt 11:29-30).

1.8.11.en: It was called “neck” because of its obedience.

1.8.12.en: And her neck has become beautiful as with chains, and truly it is so.

1.8.13.en: For if the disobedience of transgression made it formerly deformed, the obedience of faith has now made it beautiful and wonderful...

1.8.14.en: Submission and obedience were called a neck, because the neck is said to receive the yoke of Christ and to offer the obedience of faith as a treasure.

1.8.15.en: Her neck, that is, her obedience, is Christ. For He Himself first was obedient unto death (Phil 2:8), and as by the disobedience of one man, that is Adam, many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one, that is Christ, shall many be made righteous (Rom 5:19).

1.8.16.en: Thus the adornment of the Church and her chain is the obedience of Christ.

1.9.0.en: Origen “My son, if sinners entice thee, consent thou not” [10].

1.9.1.en: Verses 10-19 indicate that life is full of enticements. Here we notice groups (gangs) of young people at the corners of the roads calling a young man to take part with them in an armed robbery. The wicked are zealous to deceive others so that they walk the destructive way. Sinners love company in sin, and they have a very tempting style. Therefore it is fitting for young people to be extremely careful.

1.9.2.en: He says: “Consent thou not.” They cannot cause you any harm unless you join them of your own full will. For God’s eternal purpose for man is that he exercise freedom of will, or rather that the will, which is essentially free, cannot be compelled by any power to do a certain thing. Satan himself cannot lead a person into sin unless the person agrees to it. St. John Chrysostom says that no one can harm a person unless the person harms himself.

1.10.0.en: “If they say, Come with us, let us lay wait for blood, let us lurk privily for the innocent without cause” [11].

1.10.1.en: This is the method of the wicked in all ages, which is to call others to join them in their practice of evil against the innocent. They find their pleasure not only in persecuting the godly, but also in making many others partners with them in this violence.

1.10.2.en: This saying applies to the Jewish people, who devoted all their energies, especially at the level of the religious leaders, to kill the Lord Christ, the innocent, who alone is without sin. They wanted to kill Him and seize His possessions, that is, the Church, not in order to enrich themselves with her, but to destroy her.

1.10.3.en: * He (the wise man) understood these things of the people of the Jews, and their particular crime of shedding the blood of Christ, since they thought that His citizenship was on earth only.

1.10.4.en: St. Hippolytus * What we read in Proverbs about the wicked who say, “Let us lurk privily for the innocent...” is not a mystery that cannot be understood. It needs no effort to interpret, since it applies to Christ and to what He possesses, that is, the Church. Indeed the parable in the Gospel about the wicked husbandmen shows that our Lord Jesus Christ Himself said something like it: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and let us seize on his inheritance” (Mt 21:38).

1.10.5.en: St. Augustine * Accept my advice, my friend, and be slow in doing evil and quick in your salvation. For readiness for evil and slowness in doing good are equally bad.

1.10.6.en: If you are called to rebellion, do not hasten to it.

1.10.7.en: And if it is to apostasy, leap away in flight.

1.10.8.en: If the company of the wicked says to you: “Come with us, let us lay wait for blood, let us lurk privily for the innocent without cause” [11], do not incline to them even with your ears.

1.10.9.en: By this you gain two great benefits: the other person comes to know his sin, and you deliver yourself from the company of the wicked.

1.10.10.en: If the great David says to you: “Come, let us rejoice in the Lord,” or another prophet says: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord,” or the Lord our Savior Himself says: “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest,” or “Arise, go, and thou shalt shine with splendor, and glisten more than snow, and be whiter than milk, and shine more than sapphire,” let us neither resist nor delay.

1.10.11.en: St. Gregory of Nazianzus “Let us swallow them up alive as the grave; and whole, as those that go down into the pit: We shall find all precious substance, we shall fill our houses with spoil” [12, 13].

1.10.12.en: They “hasten like death, where the earth is split open and swallows them suddenly.”

1.10.13.en: It seems that he is referring here to the destruction of an entire city, as though the wicked were saying: “Let us destroy the man and the woman and the child, and then we will stretch out our hands and carry off all their possessions and gain great spoil.”

1.10.14.en: The destructive groups liken themselves to the earth that split open to swallow Korah and his company, who offered strange fire (Num 16:30, 33), or to what is said in the Psalm: “Let death come suddenly upon them, let them go down quick into hell: for wickedness is in their dwellings, and among them” (Ps 55:15). So they swallow every person who accepts their counsel, offering a fire strange to God; instead of the fire of divine love they kindle the fire of evil and violence.

1.10.15.en: Perhaps he is referring here to the destructive groups as graves that open continually to swallow souls dead through evil without ever being satisfied! Therefore it is fitting for us to cry with the psalmist: “Unto thee will I cry, O LORD my rock; be not deaf to me, lest thou be silent to me, and I become like them that go down into the pit” (Ps 28:1). “My bed is among the dead, like the slain that lie in the grave, whom thou rememberest no more, and they are cut off from thy hand” (Ps 88:5). They want his portion to be with the devil, of whom it is said: “But thou art cast out of thy grave like an abominable branch, and as the raiment of those that are slain, thrust through with a sword, that go down to the stones of the pit; as a carcase trodden under feet” (Isa 14:19).

1.10.16.en: They will never point to the negative results of their crimes, but rather present what seem to be rewards and advantages. This is the tempting road of sin. Satan highlights what seems good, and leaves the dark side with its ugliness hidden, to be discovered too late.

1.11.0.en: “Cast in thy lot among us; let us all have one purse” [14].

1.11.1.en: How can they cast his lot among them so that he knows his portion, and at the same time all of them have one purse? In simplicity they assure him of two things. First, that he will be as one of them; they will not wrong him in anything, but he will receive his portion by lot like them. And at the same time he will not be left in need of anything, since they have one purse, from which each takes according to his need.

1.12.0.en: “My son, walk not thou in the way with them; refrain thy foot from their path” [15].

1.12.1.en: This verse points to two ways or paths, and this reminds us of the two ways of life as given in Psalm 1, the way of the righteous, which the Lord knows and loves, and the way of the wicked, which leads to the pit.

1.12.2.en: After describing the continual enticements of the wicked, the wise man gives his son good counsel and a warning, giving three reasons for it.

1.12.3.en: · The first reason for his warning is:

1.13.0.en: “For their feet run to evil, and make haste to shed blood” [16].

1.13.1.en: His words here carry a tone of speed. The two verbs “run” and “make haste” sound the bell of “emergency.” The prophet Isaiah used the same two expressions in 59:7 when describing the wicked: “Their feet run to evil, and make haste to shed blood.” So also St. Paul in Rom 3:15: “Their feet are swift to shed blood.”

1.13.2.en: · And the second reason for his warning is:

1.14.0.en: “Surely in vain the net is spread in the sight of any bird” [17].

1.14.1.en: Solomon the Wise uses this proverb in a special sense. The wicked lie in wait in secret to trap the innocent. By this alone they hope to destroy them and seize them, because if their plans are known, the innocent will take their guard against them. For the nets are spread in vain before the eyes of the birds that a man wants to catch.

1.14.2.en: · And the third reason for his warning is:

1.15.0.en: “And they lay wait for their own blood; they lurk privily for their own lives” [18].

1.15.1.en: The wicked reap what they sow. Those who lie in wait lie in wait for themselves, where they fall into the trap. And those who attack in hidden places only attack themselves. Evil plans explode and bring evil news to the criminals, while good news is given to the one who resists these deeds.

1.16.0.en: “So are the ways of every one that is greedy of gain; which taketh away the life of the owners thereof” [19].

1.16.1.en: Solomon the Wise warns us against trying to get rich by violence or deceit. For covetousness is the sin of every hour.

1.16.2.en: * You are a captive of your money and a slave to it; you are bound with the chains and fetters of covetousness; you whom Christ once loosed have come into harsher bonds. You keep your money, which, while you keep it, does not keep you.

1.16.3.en: St. Cyprian the Martyr In brief the wise man presents us with a picture of the evil friend, summed up in the following points: 1. A flatterer who entices his friend [10]: outwardly he seems gentle, but inwardly he offers poison. 2. Within him is violence: “Let us lay wait for blood” [11]. 3. He plans [12]. 4. He is greedy [13]. 5. He sets a snare for himself without knowing it.

1.17.0.en: 20 Wisdom crieth without; she uttereth her voice in the streets: 21 She crieth in the chief place of concourse, in the openings of the gates: in the city she uttereth her words, saying, 22 How long, ye simple ones, will ye love simplicity? and the scorners delight in their scorning, and fools hate knowledge? 23 Turn you at my reproof: behold, I will pour out my spirit unto you, I will make known my words unto you. 24 Because I have called, and ye refused; I have stretched out my hand, and no man regarded; 25 But ye have set at nought all my counsel, and would none of my reproof: 26 I also will laugh at your calamity; I will mock when your fear cometh; 27 When your fear cometh as desolation, and your destruction cometh as a whirlwind; when distress and anguish cometh upon you. 28 Then shall they call upon me, but I will not answer; they shall seek me early, but they shall not find me: 29 For that they hated knowledge, and did not choose the fear of the LORD: 30 They would none of my counsel: they despised all my reproof. 31 Therefore shall they eat of the fruit of their own way, and be filled with their own devices. 32 For the turning away of the simple shall slay them, and the prosperity of fools shall destroy them. 33 But whoso hearkeneth unto me shall dwell safely, and shall be quiet from fear of evil.

1.17.1.en: In (Prov 1:20; 8:1; 9:3) Wisdom presents an invitation. It is as though both wisdom and folly seek followers for themselves, but in general we see wisdom making her call openly in the streets, and in the squares and entrances of the city, while folly and the inclination to evil are hidden and secret. Wisdom stands crying with a loud voice in important strategic places so that everyone may hear her voice.

1.17.2.en: “Wisdom crieth without; she uttereth her voice in the streets” [20].

1.17.3.en: Here wisdom appears as a person, and her voice stands in contrast to the voice of the deceitful wicked, those who were referred to earlier in verses [10-19]. This voice is heard in every place, in public and private places, in the streets as in the private room.

1.17.4.en: “She crieth in the chief place of concourse, in the openings of the gates: in the city she uttereth her words, saying:

1.18.0.en: How long, ye simple ones, will ye love simplicity? and the scorners delight in their scorning, and fools hate knowledge?” [21-22].

1.18.1.en: Man often complains that God speaks to him from His heavens, not feeling human weakness and not touching life on earth. But here we find the wisdom of God coming down to the chief places of the markets, at the entrances of the gates, where people carry on their social relations. At the entrances of the city gates the leaders used to gather for judgment (Prov 31:23; Ruth 4:11; Job 29:7), and at the heads of the markets the merchants and the people gather together for commercial dealings. It is as though the wisdom of God meets people in the reality of life, in the councils of judgment as in the markets, to lead them to practical truth. The wisdom of God incarnate, Jesus Christ, came down to us and dwelt among us as one of us.

1.18.2.en: Since Solomon the Wise showed how dangerous it is to listen to the voice of the devil, he declares here the danger of not listening to the calls of Christ as the wisdom of God.

1.18.3.en: The Book of Wisdom points to four kinds of fools, of whom we spoke in the introduction (Prov 20-21), and here the Lord Christ calls three of them: 1. The simple or the ignorant, pethayim: these cannot distinguish accurately between truth and falsehood, because they lack the ability to discern. They can easily be deceived because they are naive, and it is easy to influence them in good matters as in evil. 2. The scorners: proud and mocking people, who turn everything into a jest. They laugh at wisdom and make light of her counsel. In their view nothing is holy or serious. When someone warns them of the evil they are committing they say: “This will not happen to us.” 3. The fools: they hate learning, and carry a deep hatred of godliness. By their own will they are ignorant of wisdom, and live according to their desire. They do not care at all whether a thing is good or evil. All that matters to them is: “What does it profit me in this matter?” 4. The rebels: they hate wisdom so that it can be said that they are unbelievers and revolutionaries.

1.19.0.en: behold, I will pour out my spirit unto you, I will make known my words unto you” [23].

1.19.1.en: The phrase “Turn you at my reproof” can be understood in two ways.

1.19.2.en: The first perhaps means: Since you did not want to listen to my call, return now and listen to my reproof. I pour out my Spirit upon you so that you may discover my judgment that comes upon you.

1.19.3.en: And the second meaning is: Turn back and repent at my reproof. I pour out my Spirit upon you to help you in your repentance.

1.20.0.en: “Because I have called, and ye refused; I have stretched out my hand, and no man regarded” [24].

1.21.0.en: “But ye have set at nought all my counsel, and would none of my reproof” [25].

1.21.1.en: It is a catastrophe that God wants us to be wise and we do not want to. Man’s rejection of divine wisdom makes him stubborn, and he even becomes as though he were an irrational being. In ancient times Israel rejected God (Isa 1:4; 5:24), and in the New Testament they rejected the Savior (Mt 23:37). He spreads out His hands continually (Isa 65: 2).

1.22.0.en: “I also will laugh at your calamity; I will mock when your fear cometh” [26].

1.23.0.en: “When your fear cometh as desolation, and your destruction cometh as a whirlwind; when distress and anguish cometh upon you” [27].

1.23.1.en: It seems that these words and those that follow concern those described earlier in verses 10-19, those who refuse to turn back from their evil ways until they fall into the grasp of divine justice.

1.23.2.en: The laughter here carries no trace of cruelty or vengeance, but is symbolic language that reveals the folly of the man who mocks Almighty God, and so is like an insect mocking the flame of a fire.

1.23.3.en: They have come to the doors of entering into suffering from the requirements of the law. They must die, because their crimes have become against them, and justice leaves them in the hands of their iniquities, which know no mercy. Their ruin becomes like a tempest, like the blowing of an opposing wind.

1.23.4.en: Truly the love of Christ and the divine promises, mingled together with His reproofs, ought to be the concern of everyone.

1.23.5.en: Now sinners live the easy life, but their catastrophe is coming. Now God is ready to listen to their prayers, but afterwards they will cry in vain. Do we still despise wisdom? Let us listen diligently and obey our Lord Jesus Christ, that we may enjoy peace and confidence in God, be freed from evil in this life, and enjoy eternal glory.

1.24.0.en: “Then shall they call upon me, but I will not answer; they shall seek me early, but they shall not find me” [28].

1.24.1.en: * Many call upon Him, but not in truth.

1.24.2.en: St. Augustine If God loves sinners, it is for their repentance, their sanctification and their glory by returning to Him; therefore He refuses to listen to sinners who persist in not repenting, as He did with Israel (Deut 1:45; Isa 1:15). They seek Him early not to enjoy Him, but to obtain temporal blessings without enjoying Him; therefore they will not find Him, for whoever finds wisdom finds life and blessing (Prov 3:13; 8:17, 35). By rejecting their prayers He urges them to return to Him, that they may find in Him their resurrection from death, their eternal glory, their lasting joy and their inner satisfaction.

1.25.0.en: “For that they hated knowledge, and did not choose the fear of the LORD” [29].

1.25.1.en: The present life is a period of testing, but in eternity life becomes fixed and permanent without change; there the guilty remain guilty forever.

1.25.2.en: May no one harden his heart because of God’s longsuffering, for if he dies in his sins he will no longer be with God. And when the unquenchable fires close upon him he will not ask for mercy, for he sees clearly and feels that his hope of salvation has been utterly cut off.

1.26.0.en: “Therefore shall they eat of the fruit of their own way, and be filled with their own devices” [31].

1.26.1.en: Every person is to determine his choices in life, but he is not free to choose the results of these choices; what he sows, that he reaps (Gal 6:7; Prov 18:20; 31:31; Isa 3:10). We often hear of God who takes vengeance or who puts to death. He speaks with us in our human language. But God, who is all love and the giver of life, has no pleasure in the death of the sinner, but that he turn and live. The one who takes vengeance or puts to death is in fact our sins, which bring their fruit. When God removes His grace from us He lifts His mercies, and since we persist in not responding to Him, we drink from the cup of our works.

1.27.0.en: “For the turning away of the simple shall slay them, and the prosperity (wealth) of fools shall destroy them” [32].

1.27.1.en: This testimony became against them, when, in their wealth and in what they thought was safety for them, they were easily drawn to the fruit of their iniquities and lost their lives.

1.27.2.en: * For it is under the symbol of the Edomites, who allowed themselves to be defeated by the abundance of their wealth.

1.27.3.en: Those who rejoice in the success of this world are rebuked with the words: “Which have appointed my land into their possession with the joy of all their heart and mind” (Ezek 36:5). It is noticed in these words that they were rebuked severely, not only because they rejoice, but because they rejoice with all the heart and mind. Therefore Solomon says: “For the turning away of the simple shall slay them, and the wealth of fools shall destroy them” [32]. Paul counsels us, saying: “They that buy, as though they possessed not; and they that use this world, as not using it” (1 Cor 7:30, 31).

1.28.0.en: “But whoso hearkeneth unto me shall dwell safely, and shall be quiet from fear of evil” [33].

1.28.1.en: Among the surpassing gifts of God is inner security, for we find in Him a fortress for our depths, and so we are in Him as in dwellings of peace. This is what He promised before: “And my people shall dwell in a peaceable habitation, and in sure dwellings, and in quiet resting places” (Isa 32:18). The secret of this tranquility is the overflow of His spiritual goods upon us together with our release from the captivity of sin: “And the tree of the field shall yield her fruit, and the earth shall yield her increase, and they shall be safe in their land, and shall know that I am the LORD, when I have broken the bands of their yoke, and delivered them out of the hand of those that served themselves of them” (Ex 34:27).
